```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(simFastBOIN)
```

## What the package does

The Bayesian optimal interval (BOIN) design assigns a cohort of patients to a
dose, counts how many experienced a dose-limiting toxicity, and compares the
observed rate against two boundaries. If the rate is at or below the lower
boundary the next cohort is escalated, if it reaches the upper boundary the next
cohort is de-escalated, and otherwise the dose is repeated. The rule is as simple
to run as a 3+3 design, and Liu and Yuan report average performance comparable to
that of the continual reassessment method.

This package provides the boundaries, a fast simulation engine for operating
characteristics, and the MTD selection rule applied at the end of a trial. The
traditional 3+3 design is included as a comparator, so the two can be tabulated
side by side. For toxicity that appears late in the assessment window, the
time-to-event version of the design has a vignette of its own,
`vignette("simFastBOIN-tite")`, and so do the designs that backfill patients
to lower doses while the escalation waits, `vignette("simFastBOIN-backfill")`,
and the designs for trials of two drugs given together, which look for one
MTD combination or for the MTD contour, `vignette("simFastBOIN-combination")`.
The designs that look for the optimal biological dose, which weighs the
response against the toxicity, are described in
`vignette("simFastBOIN-boin-et")` (BOIN-ET, its time-to-event and backfill
versions, gBOIN-ET and TITE-gBOIN-ET for graded outcomes and BOIN-ETC for two
drugs) and `vignette("simFastBOIN-boin12")` (BOIN12, TITE-BOIN12, Comb-BOIN12,
TITE-Comb-BOIN12 and U-BOIN). Two extensions of the design itself are
described below: iBOIN, which brings prior information on the DLT rates into
the boundaries, and gBOIN, which decides from toxicity grades. The functions
of the section "Tables and figures" below set the results of these designs
side by side, all but the waterfall design, which selects several
combinations in a trial.

## Decision boundaries

`boin_lambda()` returns the two interval boundaries, which depend only on the
target rate and the two thresholds around it.

```{r}
boin_lambda(target = 0.30)
```

In practice the boundaries are used as whole numbers of toxicities.
`boin_boundary()` tabulates them, together with the elimination boundary, for
every attainable sample size at a dose.

```{r}
bd <- boin_boundary(target = 0.30, max_n = 18, extrasafe = TRUE)
print(bd, cohort_size = 3)
```

Reading the first column: with three patients treated, escalate on zero
toxicities, de-escalate on two or more, and stay on exactly one.

The same information can be read as a table indexed by both counts. Printing it
with a cohort size shows only the sample sizes that are actually reached.

```{r}
decisions <- boin_decision_table(target = 0.30, max_n = 18)

print(decisions, cohort_size = 3)
```

For a protocol the table is usually easier to read as a picture. Every cell
carries its decision letter, so the figure survives grayscale printing.

```{r decision-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(decisions)
```

When `extrasafe = TRUE` there is a second, stricter rule that applies at the
lowest dose only. `boin_stopping_table()` lays it out the same way.

```{r}
boin_stopping_table(bd, cohort_size = 3)
```

## Operating characteristics for one scenario

`sim_boin()` simulates the design many times under an assumed dose-toxicity
curve and summarizes the result.

```{r}
oc <- sim_boin(
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 2000,
  seed = 123
)

oc
```

The third dose is the true MTD here, and it is the dose selected most often. The
components of the result are available individually.

```{r}
oc$sel_percent
oc$percent_no_mtd
oc$overdose$pct_patients
```

## Comparing scenarios

A design is judged across a range of plausible curves rather than one.
`sim_boin_multi()` runs the same design under several scenarios and collects the
results into one table.

```{r}
scenarios <- list(
  "MTD at dose 2" = c(0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75),
  "MTD at dose 4" = c(0.02, 0.06, 0.15, 0.30, 0.50),
  "All doses toxic" = c(0.40, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75, 0.85)
)

sim_boin_multi(
  target = 0.30,
  scenarios = scenarios,
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 2000,
  seed = 123
)
```

## Design options

Six options change how the design behaves.

`titration = TRUE` treats one patient per dose until the first toxicity, which
moves through safe doses quickly.

```{r}
safe_curve <- c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.12, 0.30)

plain <- sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = safe_curve, n_cohort = 12,
                  cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, seed = 1)
titrated <- sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = safe_curve, n_cohort = 12,
                     cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, titration = TRUE, seed = 1)

rbind(plain = plain$n_pts_dose, titrated = titrated$n_pts_dose)
```

`titration_doses` ends the titration at a given dose: when no DLT is seen up
to it, full cohorts start at the next dose. With `titration_doses = 2` and
`n_earlystop = 6`, which stops the trial once six patients are at the current
dose and the design would stay, this is the accelerated BOIN design of
Kojima, Wende and Zhao (2024).

```{r}
standard <- sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = safe_curve, n_cohort = 8,
                     cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, seed = 1)
accelerated <- sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = safe_curve, n_cohort = 8,
                        cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, titration = TRUE,
                        titration_doses = 2, n_earlystop = 6, seed = 1)

round(rbind(standard = c(standard$sel_percent,
                         patients = standard$total_n_pts),
            accelerated = c(accelerated$sel_percent,
                            patients = accelerated$total_n_pts)), 1)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
kojima <- utils::read.csv(system.file("reproduce", "results",
                                      "reproduce_Kojima2024.csv",
                                      package = "simFastBOIN"),
                          stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
kojima_aboin <- kojima[kojima$design == "ABOIN", ]
```

With at most 24 patients, the accelerated design treats
`r round(accelerated$total_n_pts, 1)` patients on average against
`r round(standard$total_n_pts, 1)` for the standard design.
`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Kojima2024.R` compares it with Tables 1 and 2 of
the article: `r sum(kojima_aboin$judgement == "PASS")` of the
`r nrow(kojima_aboin)` values of the accelerated design lie within four
standard errors of the published ones.

`extrasafe = TRUE` adds a stopping rule at the lowest dose that is easier to
trigger than elimination, and `bound_mtd = TRUE` refuses to select a dose whose
estimated toxicity exceeds the de-escalation boundary.

```{r}
toxic_curve <- c(0.35, 0.45, 0.55, 0.65, 0.75)

c(
  plain = sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = toxic_curve, n_cohort = 12,
                   cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, seed = 2)$percent_no_mtd,
  extrasafe = sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = toxic_curve, n_cohort = 12,
                       cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, extrasafe = TRUE,
                       seed = 2)$percent_no_mtd
)
```

`n_earlystop` stops a trial once the current dose has accrued this many patients
and the design would stay there, which is taken as a sign that the algorithm has
settled. It defaults to 18. Note that the reference
implementation in the BOIN package defaults to 100, which effectively switches
the rule off, so a comparison between the two should set it explicitly.

For some target rates one DLT out of three patients de-escalates the dose, where
the 3+3 design would stay. `stay_on_1_of_3 = TRUE` aligns the design with that
practice by raising the de-escalation boundary at three patients, which changes
one cell of the table and nothing else.

```{r}
c(default = boin_decision_table(0.25, 9)["1", "3"],
  modified = boin_decision_table(0.25, 9, stay_on_1_of_3 = TRUE)["1", "3"])
```

## Prior information on the DLT rates: iBOIN

The iBOIN design of Zhou, Lee, Wang, Bailey and Yuan (2021) brings into the
boundaries what is known about the doses before the trial, for example from
a trial of the same drug in another population. The prior information is a
skeleton, a prior DLT rate for every dose, and a prior effective sample size
(`prior_ess`), the number of patients that the prior is worth. The
boundaries then depend on the dose: they move towards the decision that the
skeleton favors, by an amount that decreases as patients are treated at the
dose, so that the data override the prior as they accumulate.
`iboin_boundary()` tabulates them; with this skeleton and a prior effective
sample size of 3 they are the boundaries of Table 1 of the article.

```{r}
skeleton <- c(0.10, 0.19, 0.30, 0.42, 0.54)
ibd <- iboin_boundary(target = 0.30, skeleton = skeleton, prior_ess = 3,
                      max_n = 30)
print(ibd, cohort_size = 3)
```

Where the BOIN design stays on one DLT out of three patients, the iBOIN
design with this prior escalates from dose 1, whose skeleton value lies well
below the target, and de-escalates from dose 5, whose skeleton value lies
well above it. Dose elimination and the stopping rule of `extrasafe` keep
the uniform prior of the BOIN design, so that a misleading skeleton cannot
weaken them. Titration is not available.

Scenarios 3 and 9 of the article show what the prior gains and what it can
cost. In Scenario 3 the skeleton above puts the prior MTD, the dose whose
skeleton value is closest to the target, at the true MTD, dose 3; in
Scenario 9 the skeleton puts it at dose 3, two doses below the true MTD. The
trials have 30 patients in cohorts of three and are not stopped early, as in
the article, and a prior effective sample size of 0 gives the BOIN design.

```{r}
zhou <- list(
  "Scenario 3" = list(p_true = c(0.08, 0.15, 0.31, 0.45, 0.55),
                      skeleton = c(0.10, 0.19, 0.30, 0.42, 0.54), mtd = 3),
  "Scenario 9" = list(p_true = c(0.04, 0.08, 0.10, 0.18, 0.27),
                      skeleton = c(0.04, 0.09, 0.30, 0.40, 0.45), mtd = 5)
)
correct <- sapply(zhou, function(s) {
  run <- function(...) {
    oc <- sim_iboin(target = 0.30, p_true = s$p_true, skeleton = s$skeleton,
                    n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, n_earlystop = 100,
                    n_trials = 2000, seed = 123, ...)
    unname(oc$sel_percent[s$mtd])
  }
  c(BOIN = run(prior_ess = 0), iBOIN = run(prior_ess = 3),
    "iBOIN, robust prior" = run(prior_ess = 3, robust = TRUE),
    "iBOIN, MTD from the data" = run(prior_ess = 3,
                                     select_with_prior = FALSE))
})
round(correct, 1)
```

The table gives the percentage of trials selecting the true MTD. With the
right prior, iBOIN selects it in
`r round(correct["iBOIN", "Scenario 3"], 1)` percent of the trials against
`r round(correct["BOIN", "Scenario 3"], 1)` for BOIN; with the misleading
one, in `r round(correct["iBOIN", "Scenario 9"], 1)` percent against
`r round(correct["BOIN", "Scenario 9"], 1)`. The robust prior of the article
(`robust = TRUE`) sets the prior effective sample size of the doses above
the prior MTD to 0 when the number of the prior MTD is at least half the
number of doses, as in both scenarios here, which removes most of the loss.

At the end of the trial the article gives two estimates of the DLT rates for
the selection of the MTD, with and without the prior information, and does
not say which one its simulations use. They are reproduced with the prior
information, the default of `sim_iboin()` and `iboin_select_mtd()`.
Selecting the MTD from the data alone (`select_with_prior = FALSE`) gives up
part of the gain when the prior is right and part of the loss when it is
wrong.

```{r, include = FALSE}
read_result <- function(dir, file) {
  utils::read.csv(system.file(dir, "results", file, package = "simFastBOIN"),
                  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
n_pass <- function(x) sum(x$judgement == "PASS")
n_explained <- function(x) sum(x$judgement == "EXPLAINED")
n_fail <- function(x) sum(x$judgement == "FAIL")

z21 <- read_result("reproduce", "reproduce_Zhou2021.csv")
z21_t1 <- z21[grepl("^Table 1", z21$item), ]
z21_sim <- z21[grepl("^Scenario", z21$item) &
                 z21$design %in% c("BOIN", "iBOIN", "iBOINR"), ]
z21_other <- z21_sim[z21_sim$judgement != "PASS", ]
z21_other_scenarios <- paste(unique(sub("^Scenario ", "", z21_other$item)),
                             collapse = " and ")
```

`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Zhou2021.R` compares the package with the
article. `iboin_boundary()` gives `r n_pass(z21_t1)` of the
`r nrow(z21_t1)` boundaries of Table 1 exactly, and of the
`r nrow(z21_sim)` values of the rows BOIN, iBOIN and iBOINR of Table S.1 of
its supporting information, `r n_pass(z21_sim)` lie within simulation
error. The `r n_explained(z21_sim)` explained values are the percentages of
patients above the MTD in Scenarios `r z21_other_scenarios`, where the
published values agree with the percentage of patients treated at doses
whose true DLT rate exceeds 0.40. The trials agree exactly with an
implementation written in Python and fed with the same random numbers, and
without prior information they are those of `sim_boin()` for the same seed.

## Toxicity grades: gBOIN

The gBOIN design of Mu, Yuan, Xu, Mandrekar and Yin (2019) decides from the
grade of the toxicity rather than from the DLT alone. Every grade carries a
score, such as the equivalent toxicity score (ETS): 0 for grades 0 and 1, 0.5
for grade 2, 1 for grade 3 and 1.5 for grade 4. The scores are divided by
their maximum, so that they lie between 0 and 1 and count like fractions of
a DLT, and the mean score of the patients at the current dose takes the
place of the observed DLT rate, with the boundaries of the BOIN design for
the target. The target is on the same scale: a target ETS of 0.47 is a
target of 0.47 / 1.5 = `r round(0.47 / 1.5, 3)`.

The true probabilities of the grades form a matrix with one row per grade
and one column per dose. Scenario 1 of the article has six doses and 30
patients in cohorts of three, without early stopping.

```{r}
p_grade <- rbind(
  "Grade 0-1" = c(0.83, 0.75, 0.62, 0.51, 0.34, 0.19),
  "Grade 2" = c(0.12, 0.15, 0.18, 0.19, 0.16, 0.11),
  "Grade 3" = c(0.04, 0.07, 0.11, 0.14, 0.15, 0.11),
  "Grade 4" = c(0.01, 0.03, 0.09, 0.16, 0.35, 0.59)
)
oc_grade <- sim_gboin(target = 0.47 / 1.5, p_grade = p_grade,
                      score = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5), n_cohort = 10,
                      cohort_size = 3, n_earlystop = 100, n_trials = 2000,
                      seed = 123)
oc_grade
round(oc_grade$n_grade_dose, 2)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
mtd_grade <- which.min(abs(oc_grade$p_true - 0.47 / 1.5))
```

The true mean normalized scores of the doses are
`r paste(format(round(oc_grade$p_true, 3), nsmall = 3), collapse = ", ")`,
so that dose `r mtd_grade` is the MTD; it is selected in
`r round(unname(oc_grade$sel_percent[mtd_grade]), 1)` percent of the trials.
The last table gives the average number of patients of every grade at every
dose.

A dose with at least three patients is eliminated, with every higher dose,
when the posterior probability that its mean score exceeds the target is
above `cutoff_eli`, evaluated at the total score (`elim_rule = "posterior"`,
the rule of the article). The 'UnifiedDoseFinding' package applies instead
the elimination boundary of the number of DLTs to the total score, which
eliminates a dose a little later; `elim_rule = "count"` gives its rule, for
comparisons with it. With two grades scored 0 and 1 the design is the BOIN
design, and for the same seed the trials are those of `sim_boin()`:

```{r}
p_dlt <- c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60)
oc_two <- sim_gboin(target = 0.30, p_grade = rbind(1 - p_dlt, p_dlt),
                    score = c(0, 1), n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3,
                    n_trials = 1000, seed = 123)
oc_bin <- sim_boin(target = 0.30, p_true = p_dlt, n_cohort = 10,
                   cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 1000, seed = 123)
identical(oc_two$sel_percent, oc_bin$sel_percent)
```

The continuous end points of the article are not provided.

```{r, include = FALSE}
mu <- read_result("reproduce", "reproduce_Mu2019.csv")
mu_bd <- mu[mu$item == "Table 2", ]
mu_sim <- mu[mu$design == "gBOIN" & grepl("^Scenario", mu$item), ]
mu_fail_10 <- sum(mu_sim$judgement == "FAIL" & mu_sim$item == "Scenario 10")
udf <- read_result("validation", "compare-with-UnifiedDoseFinding.csv")
udf_count <- udf[udf$design == "elim_rule = count", ]
```

`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Mu2019.R` reproduces `r n_pass(mu_bd)` of the
`r nrow(mu_bd)` boundaries of Table 2 of the article and compares the
selection percentages and the numbers of patients of its Table 5 with
simulations: `r n_pass(mu_sim)` of the `r nrow(mu_sim)` cells lie within
simulation error and `r n_explained(mu_sim)` hold misprints. The other
`r n_fail(mu_sim)`, `r mu_fail_10` of them in Scenario 10, do not agree for
a reason that was not found. With `elim_rule = "count"`,
`r n_pass(udf_count)` of the `r nrow(udf_count)` values of
`inst/validation/compare-with-UnifiedDoseFinding.R` agree with the
'UnifiedDoseFinding' package within simulation error. The trials agree
exactly with an implementation written in Python and fed with the same
random numbers.

## Working with the trial data

`boin_simulate()` returns the raw counts, which is useful when a summary other
than the built-in one is needed.

```{r}
trials <- boin_simulate(
  target = 0.30,
  p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60),
  n_cohort = 10,
  cohort_size = 3,
  n_trials = 1000,
  seed = 123
)

trials
```

The MTD selection rule can then be applied separately, which makes it possible to
compare selection rules on one set of simulated trials.

```{r}
free <- boin_select_mtd(trials$n_pts, trials$n_tox, target = 0.30)
bounded <- boin_select_mtd(trials$n_pts, trials$n_tox, target = 0.30,
                           bound_mtd = TRUE)

table(free$mtd, bounded$mtd, useNA = "ifany")
```

The estimated dose-toxicity curve behind those decisions is available on its own.

```{r}
round(boin_isotonic(trials$n_pts[1:5, ], trials$n_tox[1:5, ]), 3)
```

## Comparing with the 3+3 design

`oc_3p3()` gives the operating characteristics of the traditional 3+3 design.
The probability of every path the design can take is evaluated in closed form, so
the result carries no Monte Carlo error and takes no seed.

```{r}
oc_3p3(p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.45, 0.60))
```

Two definitions of the MTD are in common use and `mtd_rule` chooses between
them. The default, `"previous"`, names the dose below the one declared too toxic.
The other takes the MTD to be the highest dose at which at most one of six
patients had a DLT, expanding a dose that has only three patients before
assessing it.

```{r}
expanded <- oc_3p3(p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.45, 0.60),
                   mtd_rule = "expand")

round(expanded$sel_percent, 1)
round(expanded$total_n_pts, 2)
```

The components of the result carry the same names as those of `sim_boin()`, so
the same code can tabulate either design. `sim_3p3()` simulates the same design
and exists to confirm the closed form rather than to obtain the numbers.

`decision_table_3p3()` shows the rule itself. With `mtd_rule = "expand"` it
also lists the search for the MTD that follows escalation.

```{r}
decision_table_3p3(mtd_rule = "expand")
```

## Tables and figures

`oc_scenarios()` tabulates the true DLT rates of the scenarios with their true
MTDs (and, when response rates are given, the true utilities and OBDs).
`oc_results()` collects the results of any of the simulation functions, of
their `_multi` versions and of `oc_3p3()` in one long data frame, and
`oc_compare()` judges them against the true doses: how often the true MTD or
OBD is selected, how many patients are treated there, how often an overdose
is selected and how many patients are treated at overdoses. All three have
`print()` and `plot()` methods. The 3+3 design is given as a list of
`oc_3p3()` results named by the scenarios.

```{r}
scenarios_two <- scenarios[c("MTD at dose 2", "MTD at dose 4")]
truth <- oc_scenarios(scenarios_two, target = 0.30)
truth

boin_two <- sim_boin_multi(target = 0.30, scenarios = scenarios_two,
                           n_cohort = 10, cohort_size = 3, n_trials = 2000,
                           seed = 123)
three_two <- lapply(scenarios_two, function(p) oc_3p3(p_true = p))

results <- oc_results(BOIN = boin_two, "3+3" = three_two)
comparison <- oc_compare(BOIN = boin_two, "3+3" = three_two, truth = truth)
comparison
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
correct_4 <- function(design) {
  comparison$pct_correct[comparison$design == design &
                           comparison$scenario == "MTD at dose 4"]
}
```

When the MTD is dose 4, BOIN selects it in `r round(correct_4("BOIN"), 1)`
percent of the trials and the 3+3 design in `r round(correct_4("3+3"), 1)`
percent. The selection of every dose is drawn by the `plot()` method of
`oc_results()`, and the comparison by that of `oc_compare()`.

```{r results-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(results)
```

```{r compare-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)}
plot(comparison)
```

## Agreement with the BOIN package

The engine draws one uniform variate per patient, in enrollment order, and
applies the decision rules in the order used by `BOIN::get.oc()`. With the
same seed and matching arguments the two implementations agree trial by trial,
not merely on average. The package's test suite checks this directly whenever the
BOIN package is installed, and `inst/validation/compare-with-BOIN.R` runs the
same comparison over 200 configurations covering every combination of the options
the two packages share.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
reference <- BOIN::get.oc(
  target = 0.30, p.true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.45, 0.60),
  ncohort = 20, cohortsize = 3, n.earlystop = 18,
  ntrial = 1000, seed = 6
)

ours <- sim_boin(
  target = 0.30, p_true = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.25, 0.45, 0.60),
  n_cohort = 20, cohort_size = 3, n_earlystop = 18,
  n_trials = 1000, seed = 6
)

all.equal(unname(ours$sel_percent), reference$selpercent)
all.equal(unname(ours$n_pts_dose), reference$npatients)
```

Clinical Trials. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series C*, 64,
507-523.

Mu, R., Yuan, Y., Xu, J., Mandrekar, S. J. and Yin, J. (2019). gBOIN: a
unified model-assisted phase I trial design accounting for toxicity grades,
and binary or continuous end points. *Journal of the Royal Statistical
Society: Series C*, 68, 289-308.

Yan, F., Zhang, L., Zhou, Y., Pan, H., Liu, S. and Yuan, Y. (2020). BOIN: An R
Package for Designing Single-Agent and Drug-Combination Dose-Finding Trials Using
Bayesian Optimal Interval Designs. *Journal of Statistical Software*, 94(13),
1-32.

Zhou, Y., Lee, J. J., Wang, S., Bailey, S. and Yuan, Y. (2021). Incorporating
historical information to improve phase I clinical trials. *Pharmaceutical
Statistics*, 20, 1017-1034.
